name: Split over slavery
description: The Methodist Episcopal Church, South formed in 1845 after a split over slavery.
narrative: The Methodist Episcopal Church, South formed in 1845 after a split over slavery. The 1844 conflict over slavery and episcopal authority led to separate southern organization in 1845. The resulting church preserved much Methodist doctrine while institutionalizing a sectional division tied to slaveholding. It entered the 1939 union with northern Methodists and Methodist Protestants. Explaining this as merely administrative geography would obscure the moral and political conflict behind the separation.

key_figures.name: John Wesley
key_figures.role: theological ancestor rather than founder of the southern separation
key_figures.summary: An Anglican minister and organizer of Methodist societies who linked the message of grace to disciplined discipleship and growth in love.

key_figures.name: James Osgood Andrew
key_figures.role: Bishop central to the slavery controversy
key_figures.summary: A Methodist bishop whose slaveholding became a focal point in the sectional conflict. His place in the story helps explain why shared Methodist doctrine did not prevent a split over slavery and episcopal authority.

name: Separation from MEC
description: The Methodist Protestant Church separated from the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1828.
narrative: The Methodist Protestant Church separated from the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1828. Reformers dissatisfied with Methodist governance organized the Associated Methodist Churches in 1828 and adopted the Methodist Protestant name in 1830. Their dispute centered on representation and church government rather than abandonment of Wesleyan faith. Most of the body joined the 1939 Methodist union. Some official summaries compress the process to an 1828 split, so the two milestones should be distinguished.

key_figures.name: Nicholas Snethen
key_figures.role: advocate of lay representation and Methodist Protestant organizer
key_figures.summary: A Methodist minister and writer who argued for lay representation and helped organize Methodist Protestant church life.

key_figures.name: Asa Shinn
key_figures.summary: A Methodist Protestant minister and reform advocate whose preaching and writing belonged to the movement for a different form of Methodist government.

name: Reunion into Methodist Church
description: The Methodist Episcopal Church reunited in 1939 to form the Methodist Church.
narrative: The Methodist Episcopal Church reunited in 1939 to form the Methodist Church. The Methodist Episcopal Church, Methodist Episcopal Church South, and Methodist Protestant Church united in 1939. Reunion overcame longstanding sectional and governmental divisions but did not erase the history of racial exclusion in American Methodism. The combined body later joined the Evangelical United Brethren in 1968. Its identity therefore combines a new institutional union with older Wesleyan doctrinal continuity.

name: Merger into United Methodist Church
description: The Methodist Church merged with the Evangelical United Brethren Church in 1968 to form the UMC.
narrative: The Methodist Church merged with the Evangelical United Brethren Church in 1968 to form the UMC. The 1968 union brought together two American connectional churches with overlapping revival and holiness histories. United Methodism links local congregations through conferences and an episcopal system and joins personal discipleship to service and mission. Its contemporary history includes substantial disagreements and departures; the dataset’s lineage is introductory and does not yet represent all recent branches or regions.
